[00:00:00] Jordan: All right everyone hi, thanks for joining. We're gonna focus today on POC scope around capacity and autoscale — reserved g-p-u counts, bursts, and fallback behavior. Maya, do you want to kick off with the business goals?
[00:00:18] Maya: Yeah thanks Jordan. So Horizon's goal for this POC is twofold, one is performance: end-user latency and tail latency matter a lot for our live chat summarization product. Two is cost predictability — we need to evaluate reserved capacity to get stable cost for peak trading hours. We're targeting p95 under 250ms for short queries, and p99 under 500ms for longer context but that's a starting point.
[00:00:45] Carlos: To add, our traffic shape is pretty bursty — we have daily spikes around market open and close, and unpredictable bursts during incident windows. Typical steady load is ~120 reqs/sec for the feature, spiking to ~900 reqs/sec for 2-5 minutes during open. We'll share more precise histograms.
[00:01:06] Priya: Got it. That's useful. For the POC we usually size three configs: conservative (reserved for steady), blended (reserved + limited burst), and aggressive (higher reserved). We'll map each to expected throughput and latency.
[00:01:22] Maya: Perfect. Also stakeholders: myself for ML, Jacob for SRE signoff, and Evelyn for product acceptance.
[00:01:30] Jacob: We'll need to validate failover policies — if reserved pool is saturated, we either want automatic burst capacity, or fallback to a quantized smaller model, or route to a lower-cost region. What's Redwood's recommended sequence?
[00:01:46] Samir: In our experience the typical pattern is: primary reserved pool -> burst/spot capacity in same region if available -> fallback to a lower-memory model variant (e.g., 7B quantized) with degradations flagged -> finally cross-region failover if allowed by policy. We can wire automated policies and thresholds into the POC.
[00:02:05] Evelyn: For product sign-off we need a clear UX-grade criteria: acceptable quality delta when falling back, and repeatable latency improvement when scaling.
[00:02:14] Priya: We'll include quality regression checks in the benchmark — a small eval set from Maya to measure n-gram overlap and a few human inspection samples.
[00:02:23] Maya: We'll provide that.

[00:06:10] Jordan: Quick Q on billing — Horizon needs predictable monthly commitment for reserved GPUs but wants headroom for bursts. We can propose reserved commit + burst tokens billed at on-demand. Are you ok with that commercial tradeoff?
[00:06:29] Maya: Yes, but we need to know the unit economics: cost per 1M tokens at each tier to compare with running in-house.
[00:06:38] Jordan: We'll send a cost matrix in the runbook.

[00:10:02] Carlos: Traffic detail — average sequence length is ~160 tokens per request, with 5-10% long tails up to 1k tokens due to long transcripts. We do a lot of streaming responses for the real-time path.
[00:10:18] Priya: That matters for KV cache and memory per replica. For GPU sizing we need to know concurrency per replica target. Do you have a per-replica concurrency goal?
[00:10:28] Carlos: We typically aim for 16 concurrent requests per GPU for the 13B-class models, but can lower for 30B+ families. For these tests we'll try to tune to your suggested guidance.
[00:10:38] Samir: For the POC we'll suggest a sizing table: e.g., 1 x A100-80GB for baseline 13B quantized at 12 concurrency (sustained ~150 req/s), 2 x A100 for blended reserved (sustained ~300 req/s), and 6 x A100 for high-reserved scenario that covers opening spike without burst. Then define burst policy to add up to 8 more GPUs for 5 minute windows.
[00:11:05] Maya: That is helpful, can you also give memory pressure and estimated GPU utilization?
[00:11:11] Samir: Expect 65-75% GPU utilization under targeted concurrency if batching is enabled, with KV cache warm. If sequences go to 1k tokens utilization goes up and p99 latency widens — we'll show that in benchmarks.

[00:15:42] Evelyn: About fallback policy — what's the user-visible behavior if we switch to a smaller model? Do we append a banner or degrade silently?
[00:15:50] Jordan: We recommend explicit degradation signals in the API response header so the product can show a banner. For the POC we'll include a flag in the response payload and logs so you can decide.
[00:16:03] Jacob: Regarding network/security, we need VPC peering and customer-managed keys for production. For the POC, can we do a VPC peering trial or do you need public endpoints?
[00:16:17] Priya: We can run with a private VPC peering for the POC; it's more setup work but doable. For initial benchmarking we can also use a temporary secure public endpoint with mTLS while peering is set up. We'll list both options in the runbook.

[00:20:00] Maya: Let's define success criteria explicitly so there's no ambiguity. From our side: p95 <= 250ms for <200-token queries, p99 <= 800ms for full distribution, no more than 2% error rate, measurable quality regression <= 3% on the eval set when fallback happens, and ability to handle open/close spike of 900 reqs/sec for 3 minutes with graceful degradation.
[00:20:26] Priya: Good. We'll propose a measurable matrix in the runbook with thresholds and test harness instructions.

[00:24:05] Samir: For benchmarks we recommend two phases: Phase A (functional + steady load): 48-hour soak at steady mean load to confirm sustained throughput and token accounting. Phase B (stress + spike): repeated synthetic spikes based on your trace to validate autoscaling and fallback transitions. We'll instrument p50/p95/p99 and GPU metrics, plus quality checks post-fallback.
[00:24:30] Carlos: How do you handle prefix/KV cache warming across replicas during a burst? We worry about cold-start latencies.
[00:24:40] Priya: Good call. We can pre-warm KV cache via synthetic steady traffic before a high-intensity window or use shared cache warm policies; for cold-start we measure a separate cold latency bucket and we'll surface that. Pre-warming typically reduces cold-start penalty by ~40-60% depending on sequence length.

[00:28:12] Jordan: Timeline — if Horizon signs off this week on POC scope we can provision reserved trial capacity in 3 business days and run benchmarks starting the week of Nov 3. Working backwards, deliverables: runbook by Oct 24, benchmark scripts by Oct 27, security docs by Oct 24, provisioning request by Oct 29. Does that work?
[00:28:34] Maya: Yes that looks fine. We'll need an internal legal touchpoint before provisioning if burst involves spot capacity.
[00:28:43] Jordan: Noted, we'll flag spot involvement in the contract quote.

[00:33:00] Evelyn: For rollout policies during POC — we want canary behavior: route 10% traffic to fallback model first, then ramp. Can Redwood automate route weights?
[00:33:12] Samir: Yes, Redwood Console supports route weights and canary rollouts by model version. We'll provide a sample canary policy in the runbook that you can tweak.
[00:33:25] Jacob: Do you provide tracing hooks for latency attribution per token and per middleware? We want to correlate SLO breaches with network vs model compute.
[00:33:34] Priya: Yes, we expose per-token latency traces, per-request broken down by routing, queue wait, batch build, model forward pass. We'll also export traces to your existing tracing backend via OTEL.

[00:38:05] Carlos: One more technical Q — if the reserved pool is full and burst capacity is unavailable, what prevents sudden latency spikes when requests backlog? Any queue backpressure strategy?
[00:38:18] Samir: We have soft queueing with backpressure and timeouts; policy options include immediate fallback, queue with SLA-based timeouts (e.g. 200ms queue limit), or reject with 429 to trigger client retry logic. We recommend queue + fallback for best UX.
[00:38:33] Maya: We'll test both reject and degrade to see which pattern product prefers.

[00:44:00] Jordan: Ok wrapping up — to be explicit on next steps: we'll send the runbook + cost matrix, you'll share actual traffic histograms and the small eval set, we'll schedule the benchmark window and provision trial reserved capacity.
[00:44:18] Maya: Action items noted. I want to be clear on acceptance: if the POC meets performance & cost guardrails we move to a quarterly reserved commit.
[00:44:29] Jordan: Understood.

[00:50:00] Priya: Quick note on metrics we'll capture during the POC: per-route token count, p50/p95/p99 latency, GPU utilization, queue times, cache hit ratio, and fallback events. We'll provide a dashboard snapshot after Phase A.
[00:50:16] Carlos: Great — also include per-region metrics; we expect some traffic egress constraints in EU region.
[00:50:25] Samir: We'll add region-level telemetry.

[00:51:30] Jordan: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with the materials and set up the bench window.
[00:51:36] Maya: Thanks — talk soon.
